newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: De Beers meets Zaire rebels over contracts.
newsitem.headline: De Beers meets Zaire rebels over contracts.

text.p: De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd said on Monday it had held contractual talks at the weekend with Zaire's rebels who control the country's vast mineral wealth.
"We can confirm that a group from De Beers was in Zaire on the weekend of April 11 to discuss contractual matters relating to the MIBA contract," De Beers spokesman Tom Tweedy told Reuters.
He gave no further details of the talks which took place in Goma.
De Beers held a contract with President Mobutu Sese Seko's embattled government to buy the output from MIBA, La Miniere de Bakwanga -- Zaire's state diamond company.
Laurent Kabila's rebel forces, who now control over half of Zaire, said earlier on Monday it planned to renegotiate contracts with international mining companies.
In the short-term, foreign companies would be allowed to continue working under existing terms.
Kabila's financial commissioner (finance minister) Mwana Nanga Mawampanga told reporters in Lubumbashi these arrangements would soon be overhauled and put on a more equitable basis.

"But at some point we are going to look at the fine print and make sure that we improve contracts where they can be improved... In other words we want to renegotiate in good faith to improve these contracts wherever possible," he said.
Mawampanga said he was not happy with De Beers' monopoly position in the diamond industry.
"It is a monopoly and we don't want monopolies in this country anymore," he told a news conference.
"If they don't want to accept that, they will have to make up their own minds what to do. We will not tolerate monopolistic behaviour in this country."
But De Beers' Tweedy said Mawampanga's comment was "odd".
"It is a bit of an odd comment about monopolies and De Beers' position... In fact there is not a monopolistic situation existing in any respect.
"We are one of a dozen or so very aggressive diamond buyers," Tweedy said.
De Beers said earlier this month that its representatives had met Kabila. It said at the time that discussions had focused on the security of its staff and facilities.
De Beers has buying offices in the rebel-held towns of Kisangani and Mbuji-Mayi and a contract to buy the production of the MIBA mine at Mbuji-Mayi.
MIBA is 80 percent owned by the Zaire government with Sibeka of Belgium owning the remaining 20 percent. De Beers holds 20 percent of Sibeka and so has a minor indirect stake in the Miba mine.
Industry sources said MIBA's diamond production was of industrial quality and worth less than $100 million a year.
But alluvial diggers accounted for about twice that.
Zaire's total official diamond production was worth around $450 million a year.
Zaire's mines ministry said last year MIBA produced around 6.5 million carats in 1996 while alluvial diggers produced about 15.4 million carats of diamonds.
